name: Valsalva maneuver bracing

card.summary: Valsalva bracing is holding the breath against a closed airway during heavy lifts to stabilise the trunk, which lifters use to train heavier and build a bigger physique.
card.note: Straining can cause dizziness, fainting or chest pain; caution is advised with heart conditions.

quick.overview:
The Valsalva maneuver is a forceful attempt to exhale against a closed airway. In lifting it is used as a bracing technique: powerlifters and Olympic weightlifters use it to stabilise the trunk in squats, deadlifts, presses and the Olympic lifts.

The appearance payoff is indirect: a stable trunk lets lifters handle heavier loads, which supports more training stimulus and, over time, more muscle.
quick.how: Lifters take a breath, hold it against a closed airway and brace through the trunk during the hardest part of a lift, then breathe out and reset. It is used on heavy compound lifts rather than light work.
quick.risks: Medical references describe a pressure rise followed by a drop on release, which can cause dizziness or fainting; chest pain or arrhythmias are possible. Caution is advised for people with coronary artery disease, valve disease or congenital heart defects. Valsalva retinopathy, bleeding in front of the retina, can occur, though vision usually recovers fully.

lead: The Valsalva maneuver is a forceful attempt to exhale against a closed airway, and in the gym it is the core of the 'brace': the lifter takes a breath, holds it against a closed glottis and tightens the trunk so the torso acts as a rigid column during a heavy lift. Lifters use it to move more weight on squats, deadlifts, presses and the Olympic lifts, and heavier loads are the route to more training stimulus and, over time, more muscle.[1][2]

The maneuver is named for the Bologna anatomist Antonio Maria Valsalva, who described the eustachian tube and used the technique to test whether it was open.[1] Wikipedia notes it is widely believed to be the best breathing pattern for maximal force, and cites a 2003 article titled 'Is the Valsalva Maneuver a Proper Breathing Technique?', which indicates the topic is still debated.[1]

Exercise physiologists have measured what the maneuver does: a 2013 review reported that it raises intra-abdominal pressure and that a Valsalva is unavoidable above roughly 80% of maximal voluntary contraction, and a 2019 systematic review found the highest abdominal pressures in squats.[2][3][2] Heavy lifting with a breath-hold also produces large blood-pressure swings, which is why cardiology references list caution for some heart conditions.[1][4][5]

chain: Breath-hold bracing raises intra-abdominal pressure and stiffens the trunk
Heavier compound lifts and more reps with good position become possible
More training stimulus and more muscle over time
angle.text: Lifters brace with the maneuver on heavy compound lifts so they can move more weight and hold position under load. Larger training loads are the route to a more muscular build.

paras: In the clinic, the maneuver is a forced exhalation against a closed airway, often with the nose pinched and the mouth closed. In lifting it is performed with a deep breath into the torso and a closed glottis while the abdominal and back muscles contract, then released after the hardest part of the rep.[1]

Lifters distinguish it from simply holding air in the chest. Forum descriptions of the brace emphasise a breath into the belly, flexing the trunk muscles 'as though you are trying to exhale forcefully', and practising it as part of the setup before the bar leaves the rack.[9][10]

Powerlifters use it to stabilise the trunk in squats, deadlifts and bench presses, and both Olympic weightlifting lifts also rely on it.[1] A T Nation reply to a lifter asking about form says bracing harder with a Valsalva would give a couple of extra reps or more weight from better core stability.[11]

Research supports the pressure effect: the 2013 review by Hackett and Chow states that the maneuver alone raises intra-abdominal pressure and that pressure increases with lifting intensity.[2] A 2019 systematic review of 16 studies from 1,125 screened reported that squats gave the highest abdominal pressure (over 200 mmHg), followed by deadlift, slide row and leg press at 161 to 176 mmHg, with the bench press lowest at 79 mmHg.[3] The authors also reported intrathoracic pressures of 105 to 130 mmHg in leg press, deadlift and box lift.[3]

subs.h: Why it is hard to avoid at heavy loads
paras: A 1992 Journal of Applied Physiology study of 31 healthy men found that blood-pressure responses to heavy lifting depended more on effort and central command than on actual force output, and the authors state that a brief Valsalva is unavoidable when the desired force exceeds about 80% of maximal voluntary contraction.[6]

Wikipedia describes the weightlifting belt as a tool lifters use to increase intra-abdominal pressure safely and to give proprioceptive feedback; it is used mainly in powerlifting and Olympic weightlifting, and commonly in squats, deadlifts and military presses.[7] It also notes that a CDC/NIOSH report found back belts had not been shown to reduce injury in industrial settings.[7]

Wikipedia describes four phases: an initial rise in pressure in the chest that squeezes blood from the lungs into the left atrium; reduced venous return, with falling stroke volume, reflex vasoconstriction and a compensatory faster pulse; a drop in pressure on release; and a rebound in cardiac output as pooled blood returns.[1] In summary, the maneuver lowers preload, with baroreflex and other reflex responses producing the changes, which is why clinicians use it to probe autonomic and cardiac function.[1][8]

Studies of blood pressure in heavy lifting predate the modern debate. A 1985 Journal of Applied Physiology study in five bodybuilders recorded a mean peak of 320/250 mmHg during the double-leg press, with one subject exceeding 480/350 mmHg, and a 1989 study using intra-arterial monitoring in eight bodybuilders recorded peaks up to 345/245 mmHg, with squats producing the highest rises.[4][5] Intra-ocular pressure was reported to rise from a mean of 13 to 28 mmHg in 11 power athletes during maximal isometric contraction.[12]

Wikipedia describes the maneuver as generally safe with rare side effects: straining can cause a drop in blood pressure leading to dizziness or fainting, and syncope, chest pain and arrhythmias have been reported. Caution is advised for people with coronary artery disease, valvular heart disease or congenital heart defects.[1]

Valsalva retinopathy, a pre-retinal hemorrhage, is associated with heavy lifting, forceful coughing, straining or vomiting; it can cause floaters and temporary visual loss, but vision usually recovers fully.[1] The 2013 review concluded that the health risks of the maneuver in resistance exercise remain unconfirmed.[2]

Lifters themselves report effects such as lightheadedness after heavy squats, exertion headaches and caution around hernias. One T Nation member linked lightheadedness to the pressure rise and rebound drop, another said exertion headaches are common in lifting and linked to the maneuver, and a member recovering from a hernia described training without Valsalva maneuvers.[13][14][15]

Beyond lifting, the maneuver is used to equalise ear pressure in diving and flying, to bring out or change heart murmurs on examination, to stop some episodes of supraventricular tachycardia, and as a standard cardiovascular autonomic test alongside deep breathing and orthostatic challenges.[1][8]

Bracing is mostly discussed on strength-training forums such as T Nation, where members describe it as a setup skill for squats and deadlifts and compare notes on side effects.[9][10][11][13] In one training log a member describes a sequence of a forceful exhale to find a neutral position, a big inhale and then a hard Valsalva as the brace, practised until it becomes part of the setup.[10]

Research on the maneuver in resistance exercise is largely physiological: the 2013 review and the 2019 systematic review measured intra-abdominal and intrathoracic pressure, and the 1985, 1989 and 1992 studies measured blood pressure during heavy lifts.[2][3][4][5][6] A 2021 study in 22 pregnant recreational lifters found placental blood flow rose slightly during a Valsalva lift rather than falling.[16]

No published trial has compared muscle growth or strength gains in lifters who brace with the maneuver against those who do not. Clinical literature otherwise uses the maneuver as a diagnostic test of autonomic and cardiac function.[8]

timeline.event: Antonio Maria Valsalva describes the eustachian tube and uses the maneuver to test whether it is open.[1]
MacDougall and colleagues record peak arterial pressures of 320/250 mmHg in bodybuilders performing heavy leg presses.[4]
Intra-arterial monitoring of bodybuilders records peaks up to 345/245 mmHg, highest in squats.[5]
A study of 31 men reports that a brief Valsalva is unavoidable above about 80% of maximal voluntary contraction.[6]
Hackett and Chow review the maneuver's effect on intra-abdominal pressure and safety in resistance exercise.[2]
A systematic review of 16 studies compares intra-abdominal and intrathoracic pressures across lifts.[3]
A 22-person study examines placental blood flow during a Valsalva lift in pregnant recreational lifters.[16]

lore.intro: Lifters on T Nation describe the Valsalva brace as a standard part of heavy squat and deadlift setup, and also trade stories about lightheadedness and headaches that follow heavy sets.[9][10][13][14]

claims.claim: Bracing with a Valsalva gives a couple of extra reps or more weight
claims.believers: A T Nation reply says bracing harder with a Valsalva will give extra reps or more weight from better core stability, and another member describes generating maximum tension with a breath and brace.[11][9]
claims.experts: Hackett and Chow report that the maneuver raises intra-abdominal pressure, and MacDougall's group states it is unavoidable above about 80% of maximal contraction; neither study measured added reps or load.[2][6]

claims.claim: The brace is an essential part of squat and deadlift technique
claims.believers: Lifters describe a setup of exhale, neutral position, big inhale and a hard Valsalva as 'your brace'.[10]
claims.experts: Wikipedia says it is widely believed to be the best breathing pattern for maximal force, and cites a debate over whether it is a proper breathing technique.[1]

claims.claim: Heavy squats and deadlifts with a Valsalva can make you lightheaded
claims.believers: A member suggests the pressure rise followed by a rebound drop could trigger lightheadedness on heavy squats.[13]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that the drop in pressure after release can cause dizziness or fainting.[1]

claims.claim: Exertion headaches are common when lifting with a Valsalva
claims.believers: A member says exertion headaches are common in lifting, especially with the maneuver, after researching them.[14]
claims.experts: A review of indomethacin-responsive headaches lists Valsalva-induced headaches such as exercise headache among primary headache disorders.[17]

claims.claim: People with a hernia or recent surgery should avoid Valsalva lifting
claims.believers: A member training through a hernia described avoiding Valsalva maneuvers and keeping every rep as perfect as possible.[15]
claims.experts: Wikipedia advises caution with the maneuver in coronary artery disease, valvular disease and congenital heart defects; it does not address hernias.[1]

claims.claim: The maneuver causes dangerous blood-pressure spikes
claims.believers: A member explains that blood pressure rises sharply when you brace hard against the abdomen.[18]
claims.experts: Intra-arterial studies recorded peak pressures of 320/250 to 345/245 mmHg in bodybuilders during heavy lifts, and the 2013 review states health risks remain unconfirmed.[2][4][5]
